sec.title: PURPOSE
sec.p: Ruxolitinib improves splenomegaly and symptoms in myelofibrosis (MF) but lacks reliable clonal burden reduction. Selinexor, an oral inhibitor of exportin 1, has demonstrated activity in MF. We evaluated selinexor plus ruxolitinib versus ruxolitinib alone in Janus kinase inhibitor–naïve MF.

sec.title: METHODS
sec.p: In this double-blind, phase III trial, patients were randomly assigned (2:1) to receive selinexor plus ruxolitinib or placebo plus ruxolitinib. Coprimary end points were spleen volume reduction ≥35% (SVR35) and absolute mean change in total symptom score (AbsTSS; excluding fatigue) from baseline to week 24.

sec.title: RESULTS
sec.p: A total of 353 patients were randomly assigned. At week 24, SVR35 was achieved in 49.8% of the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group versus 28.0% of the placebo plus ruxolitinib group (difference, 21.8 percentage points; odds ratio, 2.58 [95% CI, 1.60 to 4.17]; P < .0001). Differences were evident by week 12 and through week 36. The AbsTSS coprimary end point was not met; however, symptom scores improved from baseline in both groups (−9.9 selinexor plus ruxolitinib, −10.9 placebo plus ruxolitinib), with no significant between-group difference. At a median follow-up of approximately 12 months, the overall survival (OS) hazard ratio was 0.43 ([95% CI, 0.19 to 1.00]; nominal P = .022). Grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs) occurred in 70.1% and 50.0% of patients in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib or placebo plus ruxolitinib groups, respectively, most commonly anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia. Nausea was more frequent with selinexor but predominantly low-grade and early.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: In patients with JAK inhibitor–naïve MF, selinexor plus ruxolitinib met its coprimary end point of improved SVR35 but did not meet the AbsTSS coprimary end point, compared with placebo plus ruxolitinib. An early OS difference was observed. The safety profile was consistent with known AE profiles of the individual agents.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Myelofibrosis (MF) is a hematologic malignancy characterized by aberrant proliferation of myeloid progenitor cells, resulting in progressive bone marrow fibrosis, splenomegaly, and substantial symptom burden.1,2 Despite therapeutic advances, MF remains associated with substantial morbidity and reduced survival.3

list-item.p: Does the addition of selinexor to ruxolitinib improve spleen and symptom responses compared with ruxolitinib alone in patients with Janus kinase inhibitor–naïve myelofibrosis (MF)?

Selinexor plus ruxolitinib demonstrated higher rates of spleen volume reduction ≥35% at week 24 compared with placebo plus ruxolitinib. Total symptom scores improved from baseline and were not significantly different between treatment groups.

In this large randomized trial, selinexor in combination with ruxolitinib was shown to reduce spleen volume but did not improve symptom responses compared with ruxolitinib monotherapy. Longer-term follow-up will be important to further assess the durable clinical impact of this novel combination therapy in MF.*
*Relevance section written by JCO Associate Editor Charles Craddock, MD.

sec.p: Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors have been standard of care since ruxolitinib approval in 2011.4,5 Ruxolitinib reduces splenomegaly and improves symptoms; however, responses may be suboptimal or not durable, and treatment duration may be limited by adverse events (AEs).6-11 Furthermore, the median overall survival (OS) for patients with MF remains approximately 4-5 years,12 highlighting the need for therapies that extend beyond JAK-STAT pathway inhibition and improve long-term outcomes.

Selinexor is an oral, selective inhibitor of exportin 1 (XPO1) under investigation for the treatment of MF.13 XPO1 inhibition promotes nuclear retention and activation of tumor suppressor proteins (including p53), modulates multiple oncogenic pathways (including NF-κB–mediated proinflammatory cytokine signaling),14,15 and induces apoptosis of malignant cells.15-18 In the phase I portion of the SENTRY study, selinexor plus ruxolitinib demonstrated encouraging clinical activity (at week 24, spleen volume reduction of at least 35% [SVR35] in 79% and total symptom score [TSS] reduction of at least 50% [TSS50] in 58% of the 60-mg cohort) with evidence of biologic effects and a manageable safety profile.19

Symptom end points in MF have historically been based on TSS50, a responder end point defined as an achievement of ≥50% reduction in symptom severity from baseline as assessed by a validated tool (eg, the Myelofibrosis Symptom Assessment Form [MFSAF]). Although the use of TSS50 to assess symptom burden in phase I of SENTRY is consistent with past MF JAK inhibitor trials,6-11 the field has acknowledged the limitations of responder analyses and generally recommend using continuous versus dichotomous measurements for patient-reported outcome trial end points where possible.

Based on the phase I findings and evolving guidance on end point selection, the phase III SENTRY trial was conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of selinexor plus ruxolitinib compared with ruxolitinib alone in patients with JAK inhibitor–naïve MF, with symptom burden assessed using absolute mean change in TSS (AbsTSS), a continuous end point allowing for greater sensitivity to detect between-group differences than TSS50. Here, we report findings from the phase III SENTRY trial.

sec.title: Trial Design and Oversight
sec.p: SENTRY (XPORT-MF-034; ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04562389; EudraCT: 2020-003883-19) is a multicenter, two-part study comprising a previously reported phase I open-label portion19 and a phase III randomized, double-blind, active-controlled portion.20 This report describes the global phase III trial in JAK inhibitor–naïve adult patients with MF (Data Supplement, Fig S1, online only).

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Eligible patients were age ≥18 years with primary MF, postessential thrombocythemia MF, or postpolycythemia vera MF according to the 2016 WHO classification, as confirmed by local pathology report. Please see the Data Supplement (Supplementary Methods) for full inclusion and key exclusion criteria.

sec.title: Random Assignment and Treatment
sec.p: Patients were randomly assigned (2:1) to receive selinexor 60 mg once weekly plus ruxolitinib or placebo plus ruxolitinib. Ruxolitinib was administered twice daily per the approved product label. Random assignment was stratified by DIPSS risk category (intermediate-1 v intermediate-2 or high risk), spleen volume (<1,800 cm3 v ≥ 1,800 cm3), and baseline platelet count (100-200 × 109/L v > 200 × 109/L).

Treatment was administered in 28-day cycles. Dual antiemetic prophylaxis with a 5-hydroxytryptamine type 3 receptor antagonist and a second agent with a different mechanism of action was required during cycles 1 and 2; subsequent use was at the investigator's discretion. Dose modification guidelines were prespecified. Treatment continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal of consent, or death. If one study drug was discontinued owing to toxicity, the other could be continued until treatment discontinuation.

sec.title: End Points and Assessments
sec.p: The coprimary end points were the proportion of patients achieving SVR35 at Week 24 and AbsTSS excluding fatigue from baseline to Week 24. Spleen volume was assessed by MRI or CT within a prespecified visit window. Baseline TSS was calculated as the average of daily MFSAF v4.0 scores captured via electronic or paper diary over 7 days, with four of seven completed daily entries before treatment initiation. Average TSS was calculated every 4 weeks up to week 48 as the average of nonmissing daily TSS within the analysis window.

Secondary end points included SVR35 at week 48 and at any time, duration of SVR35 response, AbsTSS at week 48, progression-free survival (PFS, time from random assignment to disease progression or death from any cause), OS (time from random assignment to death from any cause), pharmacokinetics, and safety. Duration of response was defined from first documented response to disease progression or death. Disease progression was defined as ≥25% increase in spleen volume from nadir with loss of prior SVR35, or leukemic transformation. AEs were graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, version 5.0, and coded using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities, version 28.1, and are reported as observed within each treatment arm and may reflect contributions from either agent. Blood samples were collected at screening, weeks 24 and 48 for mutation analysis by targeted next-generation sequencing (Pillar oncoReveal Myeloid Sequencing Panel). Variant allele frequency (VAF) was assessed for all genes sequenced in the panel including the three MF-driver mutations (JAK2-V617F, CALR, and MPL). VAF percent change from baseline and proportion of patients achieving ≥20% reduction from baseline were calculated in exploratory analyses. Plasma samples were obtained at screening and at weeks 4, 24, and 48, for exploratory analyses of plasma cytokines and chemokines. Other prespecified exploratory end points and end points assessed at week 48 are described in the Data Supplement (Supplementary Methods).

sec.title: Trial Oversight
sec.p: The trial was designed by the sponsor, Karyopharm Therapeutics, and conducted in accordance with ethical principles originating from the Declaration of Helsinki and consistent with International Council for Harmonization guidelines for Good Clinical Practice. An independent data and safety monitoring committee reviewed safety data at prespecified intervals, including a nonbinding interim safety and futility analysis. The protocol and all amendments were approved by the institutional review board or independent ethics committee at each site. All patients provided written informed consent.

Data were collected by the investigators and analyzed by sponsor-employed statisticians. The manuscript was prepared by the authors with medical-writing assistance funded by the sponsor in accordance with Good Publication Practice guidelines. All authors had access to the data, critically reviewed the manuscript, and approved the submission. The authors vouch for the accuracy and completeness of the data and for fidelity of the trial to the protocol.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Efficacy analyses were performed in the intention-to-treat population, defined as all randomly assigned patients. Safety analyses included all patients who received at least one dose of study treatment.

The trial was powered for superiority with respect to the two coprimary end points at an overall one-sided type I error rate of 0.025. A sample size of approximately 350 patients provided ≥80% power for the two coprimary end points. A hierarchical testing procedure was used to control the overall one-sided type I error at 0.025, with SVR35 at week 24 tested first, followed by mean AbsTSS at week 24. If both coprimary end points were met, three key secondary end points would be tested in a prespecified hierarchical sequence to control for multiplicity: SVR35 at week 48, mean AbsTSS at week 48, and PFS (OS not included).

An odds ratio with 95% CI was calculated to assess differences in the proportion of patients achieving SVR35 between groups using a stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test adjusted for random assignment stratification factors. Nonresponder imputation was used for missing data, including missing assessments, disease progression, or initiation of new anti-MF therapy before the assessment. AbsTSS, as measured by the MFSAF v4.0 (excluding fatigue), was analyzed using a mixed-effects model for repeated measures with fixed effects for random assignment stratification factors, treatment arm, visit, treatment-by-visit interaction, baseline TSS (continuous), baseline TSS-by-visit interaction, and sex. Estimated least-squares mean differences with 95% CIs are reported.

Other binary end points were analyzed using stratified Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel tests, and continuous outcomes are summarized descriptively. Time-to-event end points were analyzed with the Kaplan-Meier method. Hazard ratios with 95% CIs were estimated with a stratified Cox proportional hazards model.

P values for the coprimary end points are one-sided; secondary and exploratory end points are not adjusted for multiple comparisons, and reported P values are nominal. CIs are two-sided and were not adjusted for multiple comparisons unless otherwise specified.

sec.p: Between December 29, 2023, and September 9, 2025, 467 patients were screened, of whom 353 were randomly assigned: 235 to selinexor plus ruxolitinib and 118 to placebo plus ruxolitinib (Fig 1).

sec.p: The median duration of treatment was 10.1 months in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and 10.4 months in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group. At data cutoff, 81.3% of patients in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and 83.1% in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group remained on study (Fig 1). The most common reasons for treatment discontinuation were withdrawal by patient (11.1% and 2.5%), AEs (8.9% and 8.5%), physician decision (7.7% and 10.2%; includes patients who proceeded to transplant), and splenic progression (6.0% and 10.2%; Fig 1). The median relative dose intensity, defined as total actual dose received divided by the total dose planned, was 86.1% for selinexor and 100.0% for placebo and was 67.7% and 83.5% for ruxolitinib in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib and placebo plus ruxolitinib groups, respectively (Data Supplement, Table S1). The median average daily dose of ruxolitinib was 23.0 and 29.9 mg/day, respectively.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: At week 24, SVR35 was achieved in 49.8% (117/235) of patients in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and 28.0% (33/118) in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group (between-group difference, 21.8 percentage points; odds ratio, 2.58 [95% CI, 1.60 to 4.17]; P < .0001; Fig 2; Table 2). The mean percent change in spleen volume at week 24 was −40.0% in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and −26.7% in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group. The treatment effect was consistent across prespecified subgroups (Fig 3). A difference in SVR35 between groups was evident at the first assessment at week 12 (49.4% [116/235] v 20.3% [24/118]) and through week 36 (Data Supplement, Table S2; Fig 2); data for week 48 were immature and are not reported.

sec.p: The AbsTSS at week 24 was −9.9 (95% CI, −11.2 to −8.6) in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and −10.9 (95% CI, −12.6 to −9.1) in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group (adjusted mean between-group difference 0.97 [95% CI, −1.07 to 3.02]; P = .825; Fig 2D; Table 2). The symptom score reductions observed in both groups were similar across symptom domains (Data Supplement, Fig S2). Prespecified subgroup analyses showed no consistent treatment effect for AbsTSS (Data Supplement, Fig S3).

At the data cutoff, the hazard ratio for duration of SVR35 response was 0.83 ([95% CI, 0.39 to 1.80]; nominal P = .33) and for PFS was 0.97 (0.61 to 1.53; nominal P = .44; Data Supplement, Table S2). At a median follow-up for OS of 11.6 months in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and 12.6 months in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group, 23 deaths had occurred (11/235 [4.7%] in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and 12/118 [10.2%] in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group; Data Supplement, Table S3). The hazard ratio for death was 0.43 ([95% CI, 0.19 to 1.00]; nominal P = .022; Data Supplement, Table S2; Fig 4). In a post hoc 24-week landmark analysis, achievement of SVR35 regardless of treatment arm predicted improved OS with 98% of SVR35 responders versus 88% of nonresponders alive at week 72 (Data Supplement, Fig S4).

sec.p: A ≥20% reduction in VAF occurred in 32.0% (54/169) of patients in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and 23.9% (22/92) of those in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group (Table 2). In a post hoc analysis comparing SVR35 responders with nonresponders regardless of treatment arm, patients with ≥20% reduction in VAF at week 24 were more likely to achieve SVR35 (odds ratio, 3.22 [95% CI, 1.81 to 5.72]; nominal one-sided P < .001).

In a post hoc analysis, selinexor plus ruxolitinib, but not placebo plus ruxolitinib, treatment was associated with a reduction in circulating peripheral blasts in patients with detectable peripheral blasts at baseline (Data Supplement, Fig S5). Conversely, more patients with 0% peripheral blasts at baseline maintained 0% through the course of treatment with selinexor plus ruxolitinib; emergence of circulating blasts was observed with placebo plus ruxolitinib, starting at approximately cycle 12. Regardless of treatment arm, absence of circulating peripheral blasts at week 24 was associated with SVR35 (odds ratio, 2.94 [95% CI, 1.62 to 5.43]; nominal P < .001).

Hemoglobin stabilization occurred in 68.9% (162/235) and 78.0% (92/118) of patients, respectively, at any time (Table 2). Other prespecified exploratory end points, including bone marrow fibrosis cytokines, additional patient-reported outcomes, and health care resource utilization showed no consistent differences between groups at the time of analysis.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: The safety population included 234 patients in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and 116 in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group (Table 3). AEs of any grade occurred in 99.1% (232/234) of patients receiving selinexor plus ruxolitinib and 97.4% (113/116) of those receiving placebo plus ruxolitinib. The most common AEs of any grade were anemia, thrombocytopenia, and nausea in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and anemia, thrombocytopenia, and constipation in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group. Grade ≥3 AEs occurred in 70.1% (164/234) and 50.0% (58/116) of patients, respectively. The most common grade ≥3 AEs in both groups were anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Rates of anemia of any grade and grade ≥3 were similar between groups. The selinexor plus ruxolitinib group had modestly higher rates of thrombocytopenia without bleeding events, a slight increase in neutropenia without evidence of excess infections or febrile neutropenia, and slightly higher fatigue. Nausea, which was predominantly grade 1 or 2, occurred more frequently in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group, and onset was most commonly reported during the first two treatment cycles (Data Supplement, Table S4). Dose modification and treatment discontinuation because of AEs were more frequent in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group (Data Supplement, Table S5). Serious AEs occurred in 26.9% (63/234) of patients in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group and 24.1% (28/116) in the placebo plus ruxolitinib group. AEs resulting in death occurred in 0.9% (2/234) of the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group (cardiopulmonary failure and drowning) and 2.6% (3/116) of the placebo plus ruxolitinib group (acute kidney injury, pleural effusion and respiratory failure, and sudden death/unknown); none were considered by investigators to be related to study treatment. Transformation to AML was infrequent and occurred at equal rates in both treatment arms (1.7% each).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: One of the two coprimary end points was met in this phase III trial involving patients with JAK inhibitor–naïve MF, where selinexor plus ruxolitinib demonstrated rapid, deep, and sustained SVRs with a significantly higher rate of SVR35 at week 24 than placebo plus ruxolitinib. Differences were evident as early as week 12 and were maintained through later time points including week 36, with consistent effects across prespecified subgroups. The coprimary end point of AbsTSS at week 24 was not met, with no significant difference between treatment groups; however, both treatment arms demonstrated symptom improvement from baseline with consistent effects across symptom domains. Fatigue was excluded from the primary symptom end point, consistent with the study design and prior precedent,21-24 given challenges in its assessment in MF and the potential for confounding by treatment-related effects, including an increase in fatigue with selinexor.

The higher rate of SVR35 with selinexor plus ruxolitinib than with ruxolitinib plus placebo did not lead to a greater improvement in AbsTSS. A few factors may be contributing to the discordant results. In prior research,7,25 SVR has been correlated with improvements in the GI-related symptoms parts of the MFSAF. Nausea is a known AE associated with selinexor and not ruxolitinib, which directly overlaps with items within the MFSAF related to GI symptoms. Thus, the AbsTSS results may be affected by instrument bias because of the safety profile of selinexor. Another factor is that ruxolitinib is very effective at reducing MF-related symptoms, to the point where further reduction in spleen volume may not lead to greater improvement in symptoms. However, improved spleen response in the absence of superior symptom response remains an important treatment goal, as SVR has been associated with improved OS.26-28

Although follow-up limits the interpretation of OS and the results should be considered hypothesis-generating, an early difference in OS was observed, a notable finding in MF, where early survival has not been seen in randomized trials so far. The 24-week post hoc landmark analysis was consistent with prior studies,7,26 including pooled analyses of ruxolitinib-treated patients, showing that spleen response predicted survival outcomes in MF, further validating the importance of achieving a spleen response.26-28 Exploratory analyses showing reductions in driver mutations VAF and decreases in peripheral blasts with selinexor plus ruxolitinib support a potential effect on the underlying malignant clone consistent with the known cytotoxic effect of XPO1 inhibition. These findings suggest that selinexor may drive early and deep spleen responses through elimination of neoplastic cells, which may be associated with improved long-term outcomes.

Ruxolitinib has been the foundation of first-line therapy for MF since 2011 and is associated with reductions in splenomegaly and MF-related symptoms; however, responses are often limited in depth and durability.6-11 The addition of selinexor enhanced SVR while maintaining symptom improvement with a safety profile consistent with the known adverse event profiles of the individual agents. Notably, higher SVR35 rates were achieved despite a lower median relative dose intensity of ruxolitinib in the selinexor plus ruxolitinib group, as observed in the phase I portion,19 supporting an independent contribution of selinexor to efficacy and potential synergy.

Although the safety profile was consistent with the individual agents, there were some notable differences between treatment arms. AEs leading to dose modification or treatment discontinuation were more frequent with selinexor plus ruxolitinib than placebo plus ruxolitinib. Grade ≥3 AEs, most commonly cytopenias, including neutropenia, were more frequent with selinexor plus ruxolitinib than placebo plus ruxolitinib. Notably, the higher neutropenia rate was not accompanied by an increase in infection or febrile neutropenia. Additionally, GI AEs, particularly nausea, were more frequent with selinexor but were largely limited to the first two cycles and predominantly low grade. AEs (eg, nausea) were generally manageable with supportive care and dose modification.

Several limitations must be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. Lack of longer follow-up for OS and other time-to-event end points limits definitive conclusions regarding long-term clinical benefit. Definitions of PFS in MF are not standardized across studies, and the relationship between PFS and OS remains incompletely characterized,7,29,30 which may further complicate interpretation of time-to-event end points in this setting. In addition, the clinical significance of exploratory molecular findings remains to be established. Interpretation of symptom endpoints may be influenced by substantial symptom improvements achieved with ruxolitinib alone, which may limit the ability to detect incremental differences between treatment groups. In addition, overlap between treatment-related AEs and MF-associated symptoms may affect assessment using patient-reported outcome instruments such as the MFSAF. Secondary and exploratory end points were not formally tested and should be interpreted with caution.

In summary, SENTRY met its coprimary end point of SVR35, but not AbsTSS. Selinexor plus ruxolitinib resulted in rapid, deep, and sustained reductions in spleen volume compared with ruxolitinib alone in patients with JAK inhibitor–naïve MF. Both groups experienced comparable symptom improvement from baseline, with no between-group differences. Taken together, the SVR35 rates, early OS difference, and molecular findings suggest a potential mechanistic link between cytotoxic targeting of the malignant clone and improved clinical outcomes, supporting selinexor plus ruxolitinib as a potential first-line therapeutic strategy in MF.
